title: Counting the Outcomes
objective: After this level you can list the equally likely outcomes of two dice and explain why 7 is the most common total.
summary: Galileo explained why three dice make 10 more often than 9 by counting throws, not sums. Two dice give 36 equally likely throws; 7 is made six ways (1 in 6), while 2 and 12 have one way each.

cards.headline: Dice players in Galileo's day noticed that three dice made 10 more often than 9.
cards.body: It seemed wrong. Each total can be built from six different sets of numbers. Galileo was asked to explain it, and his answer is the trick behind every dice chance: count the throws, not the sums.

cards.headline: Galileo counted throws, not sums
cards.body: Galileo's key move was to treat the dice as separate. One die can land 6 ways. Add a second, and each of its faces pairs with each face of the first: 6 × 6 = 36 throws. A third die makes 216. Counted that way, a total of 10 turns up in 27 of the throws and 9 in only 25. The players' long observation had been right all along; now it had a reason.

cards.headline: Two dice, 36 equal throws
cards.body: Now just two dice. Imagine one red and one blue, so a red 2 with a blue 5 is a different throw from a red 5 with a blue 2. That gives 36 equally likely throws. A total of 7 can be made six ways: 1 and 6, 2 and 5, 3 and 4, each either way round. A total of 2 needs both dice on 1, and 12 needs double 6: one way each.

cards.fact: 7 comes up 1 time in 6. Snake eyes, 1 time in 36.
cards.context: Six of the 36 throws make 7, so its chance is 6 in 36, or 1 in 6: better than any other total. A 2 (snake eyes) and a 12 get 1 in 36 each. Level 21's rule did the work: count the equally likely outcomes, then divide. The skill is making sure the things you count really are equally likely.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: the totals are not equally likely, the throws are. Count the 36 throws first, then sort them into totals.

cards.headline: Dice: counted
learned: 7 is 1 in 6, the most common total
